about: Uppsalir (Gamla Uppsala in Uppland), the Svear kings' estate, holy place and thing-place up a small river from the bay, 793 to 1066. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/uppsalir.md, the spine (threads riddle_road, cross_and_grove, price_of_england), riddles_793.json (the Svear king's skald, the hearth-keeper, the fowler, the set dellings_door) and realms/sweden_gotland.md. A draft for the user to overwrite. Three layers are kept apart: the ground (mounds, hall, grave field: real, older than 793, nameless), Adam of Bremen (about 1075, second hand) and the Icelanders and the Uppland law (LATER). Everything that leans on a late text says so, and (?) marks what is not verified. The year the great hall burned is not known: the game switches the hall for the burnt terrace at 800, and that year is the game's, not a fact.

ports.summary: Uppsalir is not a town. It is the Svear kings' estate, their holy place and the place of the great thing: a ridge with three huge mounds, a hall on a built-up terrace, a low flat mound where the law is said, and graves as far as a man can see, among farms. No quay, no mint and no toll are recorded: a boat is left where the river gives out in the wet meadows and the goods go up on backs, carts or sledges. A merchant comes to sell wine, glass, cloth, salt and blades to a king's household, to buy iron and furs when the whole people meet in late winter, and because what the thing decides here binds Birka.
ports.seasons: The bay is ice from early winter until about April and no ship moves, but in late winter, while the ice still bears, the Svear come by sledge to the thing, the market and the offering to the women who watch over the kin (LATER: Snorri). In spring the river floods the plain; ships go out in May and are home by autumn; Yule is kept at midwinter, and about the spring equinox of every ninth year, Adam of Bremen says, comes the great feast that nobody is excused.

history.text: Between about 550 and 625 three great mounds are raised on the ridge, each over a burning: seven to eleven metres high and fifty-five to seventy across. In 793 they are some two hundred years old and nobody can prove whose they are.
history.source: sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala_fornlämningsområde; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala (dossier, section 2). The names Aun, Egil and Adils are modern labels.

history.text: About this time a hall fifty to sixty metres long is built on a terrace of piled clay, with doors three metres wide and iron spirals laid in the post holes, and a row of tall posts is set across the plain, a hundred and forty-four of them in a line a kilometre long.
history.source: sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala_fornlämningsområde; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_at_Uppsala. The hall's date is from memory of Ljungkvist's digs (?); the posts are dated to the mid 400s or to about 600.

history.text: Nothing is written of Uppsalir this year or any year near it. The mounds are old. The great hall stands, or has just gone.
history.source: dossier, section 5: no text written between 793 and 1066 by anyone who stood here survives

history.text: About this year (?) the great hall on the terrace burns, so hot that the clay of its walls is fired to brick. Those who dug it read the fire as set on purpose.
history.source: sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala_fornlämningsområde; the date is from memory and not checked (?). The game switches the site at 800; no year is known.

history.text: The sons of Godfred, king of the Danes, come home from exile among the Svear and take the Danish kingdom. Where among the Svear they had lived is not written.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 813, by way of Design/content/realms/sweden_gotland.md

history.text: The monk Anskar comes to Birka and King Bjorn lets him preach. The Svear had sent to the emperor to ask for priests. Uppsalir is not named.
history.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 9-11 (tr. C. H. Robinson 1921)

history.text: In these years Anund, a king of the Svear driven out, comes against Birka with Danish ships. The town buys peace with a hundred pounds of silver, and the lots send the Danes away to rob a town of the Slavs.
history.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 19 (Robinson 1921); between 845 and 851, the year not given

history.text: King Olaf puts Anskar's request to the lots and then to the thing at Birka, and to a second thing in another part of his kingdom. Both say yes. A man says the gods have offered to take the dead King Eric among them if the people want more gods.
history.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 26-27 (Robinson 1921). Rimbert does not say where the second thing met.

history.text: After this year a Gotland farmer buries sixty-seven kilograms of silver under his floor. From about this time weights made to the measure of the caliphs' coin are common among the Svear.
history.source: The Spillings hoard, youngest coin 870/871 (riddles_793.json rw_hoard_spillings; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spillings_Hoard)

history.text: Archbishop Unni of Bremen dies at Birka on the seventeenth day of September. The mission he came to raise up lapses again.
history.source: Adam of Bremen I.62 (?), by way of Design/content/realms/sweden_gotland.md

history.text: Birka is empty by about this year. About 980 a king's town of measured plots, Sigtuna, is laid out on the water a day's row south of Uppsalir.
history.source: chronicle_793.json 975-birka-sigtuna; dendrochronology of Sigtuna's first plots

history.text: About this year King Eric beats his brother's son Styrbjorn and a fleet of Danes on the wet plain below Uppsalir. A stone in Skane says of a dead Dane that he did not flee at Uppsala. An Icelander, Thorvald Hjaltason, makes verses on the fight and the king pays him.
history.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fyrisvellir: the sagas are LATER and Lauritz Weibull doubted the battle; the rune stones DR 295 and DR 279 and the verses speak for it

history.text: About this year Olof, Eric's son, is king, and English moneyers strike pennies with his name at Sigtuna: the first coin of the Svear.
About this year (?) King Olof is baptised, in the land of the western Gotar and not here. The Svear keep their feasts.
In the early years of this century Sigvid, who had been to England, raises a stone at Uppsalir for his father Vedjarf.
history.source: Rundata U 978, now in the wall of Gamla Uppsala church: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppland_Runic_Inscription_978. The year is the game's; the stone is dated only to the early 1000s.

history.text: About this year the mint at Sigtuna stops. The Svear go back to the scales.
Ingvar's fleet is lost in the east. Twenty-six stones round the bay remember men who went with him.
history.source: The Ingvar stones (for one, Rundata So 179); Design/content/realms/sweden_gotland.md

history.text: In these years Adalvard, bishop at Sigtuna, and Egino, bishop in Skane, mean to close or burn the holy place at Uppsalir. King Stenkil forbids it: they would be killed and he driven out. Adalvard has to leave for the western Gotar.
history.source: Adam of Bremen IV.30, by way of en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adalvard_the_Younger (dossier). The year is not given: the 1060s.

history.text: King Stenkil dies. Two men named Eric fight for the kingdom and both are killed, and the bishops stay away.

eras.text: The kings' estate at its oldest: three mounds on the ridge, a hall two hundred years old on its clay terrace (the game lets it stand until about 800; no year is known), sunk houses of weavers and smiths, farms, and graves in every direction. Whose hall it is no writer says: people here say 'the king'. Heathen, no coin: silver is weighed. The market is at Birka; here there are dues, gifts and, in late winter, the whole people.

The terrace is burnt clay and the household eats in a lesser house beside it. Why the old hall was fired nobody tells a stranger. The first coins of the caliphs come up from the east and are weighed like any silver. The sons of a dead Danish king live somewhere among the Svear until 813, and then go home to take his kingdom.

The years the Franks write about, though they write of Birka. Word comes up the river of a monk who preaches there by the king's leave, of a bishop driven out about 845 and not by the king's order, of an exiled king with Danish ships and a hundred pounds of silver paid. In 852 the lots and two things say the new god may be preached. At Uppsalir the feasts are kept as before.

The mission lapses and nobody here misses it. Silver comes from the east in a flood: weights are made to the caliphs' measure and even farmers carry scales. The great are laid unburnt in boats on the hill upriver and by the estate. From 871 the king's skald keeps the first stick of a chain of riddles that ends in the ground on Gotland. About 950 the silver is at its height; after it thins.

Birka is empty and the land goes on rising: the plain is drier each lifetime and boats stop lower down. About 980 the king lays out Sigtuna on the lake, a town of plots, and a merchant now deals there with a host. About 985 a fleet comes up the river and is beaten on the plain; the dead lie where they fell for a season and the ravens are fat.

King Olof strikes pennies at Sigtuna with his own name on them, cut by an Englishman, and for the first time a price here can be counted. He is baptised about 1008, far to the south-west, and may force nobody. Men come home from England with tribute silver, and stones with crosses begin to stand by the roads. The feasts at Uppsalir are kept.

Kings Anund, Emund and Stenkil. The mint stops about 1030 and the scales come out again. A cross and a hammer hang on one neck and nobody mocks either. In the 1060s a bishop sits at Sigtuna and wants fire at Uppsalir; the king forbids it. In a ninth year a Christian still pays to stay away. In 1066 Stenkil dies and the land is at odds with itself.

sites.name: The boat place below the meadows
sites.see: In front, a low clay bank where the grey river widens for the last time: a dozen small boats drawn up among willows, oars inboard, a sledge on its side, one turf-roofed shed. Behind, flat wet meadow to the skyline, and on the skyline three round hills that are not hills. Curlews, the suck of mud, a smell of tar and wet hay.
sites.source: dossier, section 1: travellers left their boats and walked (uncited there (?)); where the boats were left is not known. The shed is invented.

sites.name: The sheds under the boat hill
sites.see: Half an hour upriver of the estate, a steep grass hill with long low hollows in its side, each the length of a boat. Under it, by the water, two open sheds, a steaming trough, split oak stacked to season and a slim boat in frame. Adze strokes, smoke, pitch. The wrights do not look at the hill while they work.
sites.source: Valsgarde, 3 km north on the river: boat graves from the 500s to the 1000s (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valsgärde). That boats were built under the hill, and that a light boat came this high, are inference (dossier, section 1) (?)

sites.name: The wet plain and the row of posts
sites.see: A trodden way of brushwood and planks runs north across flooded grass. Beside it, a line of great grey posts marches off towards the mounds, some upright and taller than a ship's mast is long, many leaning, more only stumps, with old black hearths at their feet. Cranes stand in the shallows. In late summer stallions are led out here and men lay silver on them.
sites.source: The plain flooded and its name is from fyrva, to ebb (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyrisvellir); the post rows, found 2012-2013 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_at_Uppsala). Whether any post still stood in 793 is unknown (?). The stallion fights are town_games_793.json; crane bones are from the estate's middens.

sites.name: The great hall on the terrace
sites.see: A bank of piled clay as high as two men, and on it one roof sixty paces long, its shingles silver-grey, its two side doors wide enough for a cart and bound with iron curled like fern heads. Inside, dark and warm: a long fire, benches, shields on the wall, a high seat seen through smoke. Roast pork, wet wool, wood smoke two hundred years deep.
sites.source: The hall on Kungsgardsplatan: 50-60 m by 12 m, doors 3 m wide, iron spirals (sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala_fornlämningsområde). Shown standing until 800 by the game's choice; no year is known (dossier, section 8).

sites.name: The burnt terrace and the king's house
sites.see: The clay bank is still there, and on it nothing: a floor fired red and hard as a pot, black stumps, nettles. Children are told not to play there and do. Below its north end stands the house the king eats in now, half the length of the old one, new thatch already going grey. A horn sounds for meat. Ash still blows off the terrace in a dry wind.
sites.source: The hall burned so hot the clay turned to brick (sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala_fornlämningsområde). The lesser house is invented: later halls stood where the church now is (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_at_Uppsala, the radar survey of 2005) (?)

sites.name: The guest house by the hearth-keeper's door
sites.see: A long low house below the terrace, door to the south, a rack of sledges and skis under the eaves and a midden of fish bones behind. Inside, sleeping benches along both walls, a fire kept in day and night, a vat of ale, strangers from four days' sledging in every direction drying their foot-cloths. Barley porridge, herring that has come a long way, wet dog.
sites.source: invented; cod and herring were carried up from the coast and eaten here (sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala_fornlämningsområde). That a traveller may not be refused a roof among the Svear is Adam of Bremen IV.21 (?), about 1075.

sites.name: The three mounds
sites.see: Three great round mounds in a row along the ridge, each as high as a ship's mast and grown with short grass and harebells, sheep on their sides. From the top the plain lies open to the bay, and lesser mounds run away north and east like a herd lying down. Wind, larks. Nobody stands on the middle one to talk business.
sites.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala; sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala_fornlämningsområde. Whose bones are in them is not known.

sites.name: The flat mound
sites.see: A low mound with its top cut level, east of the great three, the grass on it worn to earth by feet. In late winter it stands in trampled snow with a hazel rope round it and a thousand men about it, breath smoking, spear butts knocking on shields for yes. In summer it is a place where a lawman sits and children are chased off.
sites.source: Tingshogen, low and flat-topped (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala); its age is not known (?). The thing of all the Svear in late winter is Snorri and the Uppland law of 1296: LATER. Assent by weapon-noise and the hazel rope are from later Norse law and saga (?)

sites.name: The sledge market
sites.see: Trodden snow between the thing mound and the houses, and on it sledges drawn up in rows with their shafts in the air: bundles of grey squirrel tied in forties, bars of iron, frozen fish stacked like firewood, elk hides, wax. Men in fur caps hold folding scales at eye height. Out of the thing weeks there are six sledges, or a cart, or nobody.
sites.source: A market held with the late-winter thing for a week: Snorri, Heimskringla, Olaf the Saint's saga c. 77 (Laing 1844) (?): LATER. What was sold is not recorded; furs and iron by sledge are inference (dossier, section 4); trade_year_793.json svealand, month 2.

sites.name: The sunk houses
sites.see: Thirty small roofs that seem to sit on the ground, each over a pit a man can stand in. Through one door a row of clay weights swings on a loom as tall as the roof; through the next a bellows wheezes and a boy holds tongs. Wool grease, hot iron, charcoal. A woman at a door measures cloth along her arm and says a number twice.
sites.source: More than 30 pit houses with traces of weaving and metalwork, dug in 2012 (sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala_fornlämningsområde); their date within 500-1050 was not checked (?)

sites.name: The old trees by the spring
sites.see: A stand of very old ash and oak in a hollow east of the houses, with a spring rising dark among the roots and running off through ice or cress. No branch here has been cut in living memory; rags of wool and a horse's skull hang where the path goes in. It is quiet in a way the plain is not. In a ninth year strangers are not walked this way.
sites.source: A grove where every tree is holy and a spring are in Adam of Bremen IV.26-27 only (about 1075, second hand; no safe translation, not quoted). The game shows trees and water and never the feast (dossier, sections 6 and 8).

sites.name: The grave field
sites.see: Low grassy mounds beyond counting, shoulder to shoulder from the ridge down to the fields, some with a stone on top, some fallen in. Here and there the earth is new, and in two places it is heaped long and narrow over a boat. From about 1015 a tall red-grey stone with a snake of runes on it stands by the path. Sheep, thistles, a pyre's old black ring.
sites.source: Once 2,000-3,000 mounds; a pyre with human, horse and dog bone; boat graves by the vicarage (sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala_fornlämningsområde; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala). The stone is U 978 (runes are read with learned.runes).

sites.name: The king's new town on the lake
sites.see: A day's row south, on the way in from the bay: one long street of gravel along the shore, narrow plots running down from it to the water like the teeth of a comb, a house at the head of each and a boat at the foot. A king's yard in the middle. Hammering, pigs, fresh-cut pine. From about 995 a man at an open shutter strikes pennies; from about 1060 there is a bishop and a wooden church.
sites.source: Sigtuna, laid out about 980 (chronicle_793.json 975-birka-sigtuna); the mint about 995-1030 (act:change_coin belongs to those years only); a bishop about 1060 (Adam of Bremen IV, by way of en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adalvard_the_Younger). Sigtuna is not a port in ports_793.json: the game reaches it through Uppsalir. The guild oath is unlocks_793.json unlock_title_frisian_guild.

people.name: Vifast
people.trait: The king's poet and the keeper of the oldest lays in the north: exact, slow, and proud of being slow.
people.want: To hear every other hall's version of a lay, so that he can say where it is wrong.
people.fear: That he will die with the count of the lays unfinished, and that the Danes' poet will then say what he likes.
people.voice: Counts stanzas the way his people count skins: aloud, and twice. Never hurries an answer and thinks worse of those who do.
people.looks: About forty-five, tall and stooped, a long pale beard in two plaits, a grey cloak with a border of marten and a plain bronze ring pin, a bundle of notched tally sticks tied at his belt.
knows: the giant's questions and the High One's, stanza by stanza, at six and eight pennyweights of silver
the old kings as the lays have them, and that the lays do not agree
who sat where in the hall, and so what the king thinks of a guest
which skald in which hall holds which lay

ties.note: The Danes' poet makes new turns. Vifast says he keeps the old ones because he can still count them.
The Birka skald learned his trade on this bench and sells it by the cup to merchants, which Vifast pretends not to know.
Ravn sat a winter here as a young man after he left the Danes' hall, and was the only guest who ever corrected the count.
He sells the riddle of the embers as his own. It is hers.
The lawman keeps the law by heart and the skald keeps the lays: they test each other's memory every Yule for an ox-horn of ale.
The Birka trader brings him wax for tablets he never uses, and news, which he does.
Likbjorn, who cuts the picture stones on Gotland, trades him riddles for verses by the Gotland boats; neither will say who is ahead
a Svea on a hill over the sea sends him a pelt each year to go on telling how his fathers took tribute there; he tells it, and keeps the pelts
his daughter's daughter's son will have his tally sticks and his bench two lifetimes on, and will not be able to read all the notches

lines.greet: A Frisian. You people count coins. I count stanzas. Fifty-five in the giant's lay: I counted them this morning, and again when I saw your boat.
lines.greet_again: You are back before the ice. Good. I have a question for you and you have, I think, six pennyweights for me.
lines.greet_friend: Sit on my left. That is the side I hear with, and the side the ale comes from.
rumour: The Danes' poet at Hleidr says older is not better. He has said it to nine skippers. I have counted them.
A king here once chased a Dane across the plain, and the Dane sowed gold to slow him. Poets call gold that field's seed. Look down as you walk.
There is one question in the lay no man can answer. I do not sell it. If your grey seaman is aboard, ask him why.
lines.saying: A lay is like a fur: count it when you get it and count it again when you hand it on.
lines.farewell: Go well. If you pass Hleidr, tell their poet nothing. He will make a verse of it.

people.source: invented; 'a skald of the Svear king' who sells r-vafth-15, -17, -22, -38, -42 and t-vafth-12, -29, -39 at 6 and 8 d (riddles_793.json, texts_793.json). The gold sown on the plain is Hrolf Kraki's, from Snorri's Skaldskaparmal (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyrisvellir): LATER, told as old song. Ravn's winter here is this file's invention, tied to the spine's thread riddle_road.

people.name: Gillaug
people.trait: The woman who keeps the hall's hearth and the guest house: she has banked that fire every night for thirty winters and forgets no face that sat by it.
people.want: That the fire is never let out while she lives, whatever becomes of the roof over it.
people.fear: A cold hearth. A year with too many guests and too little barley.
people.voice: Speaks while doing something else. Asks what you ate last and where, and knows from the answer how your voyage went.
people.looks: Near fifty, broad, sleeves rolled, a brown strap dress on two worn oval brooches, a string of plain glass beads, keys and a fire-steel on her belt, hands scarred white by sparks.
knows: who is in the guest house and where they came from, by their foot-cloths
what the household lacks: salt, malt, wine for the high seat, good cloth
the riddle of the embers, which she gives for nothing to anyone who sits up with the fire
what the king's household ate this week, and so how the dues came in

ties.note: He sells her riddle. She waters his ale by exactly the worth of it.
Her sister's daughter, whom she put to the loom rather than the hearth, and tells so.
The fowler brings her the cranes first. He eats by her fire all winter for it.
A far kinswoman's line: the rich widow of Birka in the 840s is her brother's daughter's child (the game's link) (?)
Fastulf, the old island's bronze-caster, made the hall's great cauldron chain. It is not all paid for.

lines.greet: You have had nothing hot since Birka. Sit. Silver later; porridge first.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian. That bench, the dry end. You left a whetstone here last time. I have it.
lines.greet_friend: I kept the fire in for you. I keep it in for everyone, but for you I said so.
rumour: The household is short of salt and nobody will say so at table. A man with salt would be remembered by the one who cooks.
Sit up with me tonight when I bank the fire and I will show you some maidens. Grey ones. The skald charges for them.
The old roof drips on the high seat. Nobody mends a roof that old. They talk about what to do with it, in low voices.
lines.saying: A fire and a guest: feed both or lose both.
lines.farewell: Go dry. Praise the ice when you are across it, not before.

people.source: invented; 'the woman who keeps the hall's hearth' who gives r-gest-33, pale embers on the hearth (riddles_793.json). Her farewell turns Havamal 81 (Bellows 1923; texts_793.json havamal_081).

people.name: Holmgeir
people.trait: Says the law from the flat mound and holds the scales at the sledge market: a farmer of forty cows who thinks kings are a thing the people keep, like a bull.
people.want: Every weight in the land to agree with his, and the thing to end without a spear thrown.
people.fear: A king who will not ask. A year when the lots say one thing and the people shout another.
people.voice: Says each number twice and the law in threes. Does not raise his voice: he waits until the others lower theirs.
people.looks: Past fifty, thick-set, a clipped grey beard, a fur cap and a long belted coat of undyed wool, a hazel staff, folding scales in a round bronze case hung at his chest.
knows: what a stranger's life is priced at here, and that a host answers for his guest
what the thing decided on ships and men for the summer (the levy is known from later law only) (?)
the weights: he will try yours against his for a small gift
that the king puts a matter to the people and the lot, and does not command it

ties.note: The young man who will keep the port at Birka stood beside him at the thing and learned to argue in the rain.
His sister's son. They weigh each other's silver and are both pleased when it agrees.
A memory against a memory, every Yule.
He fined the fowler's father a cow, wrongly as it proved, and has not found a way to say so.
Hailgair says the law for the farmers of Gotland's west shore, and says the island asks no king's leave for it. Holmgeir asked what that costs them. He was told: nothing yet.

lines.greet: A stranger with goods. Who is your host? No host, no peace. Find one, then come and I will weigh for you. Find one.
lines.greet_again: Your silver was good last time. I tried it twice. Put it in the pan again.
lines.greet_friend: Stand by me at the mound and say nothing. It will be noticed whose shoulder you were at.
rumour: The king wants ships for the summer. He has asked. The thing has not said yes. That is the order things go in here.
A Dane or a Frisian killed in this land costs less than one of us. I did not make the law. I only remember it.
Eight parts to the mark, three to each part. Twenty-four. If a man at Birka tells you twenty-five, bring him to me.
lines.saying: The people take a king, and the people can put him down again.
lines.farewell: Go with the thing's peace as far as the boats. After the boats it is your own.

people.source: invented; the office from the lawmen of later Svea law. 'Sveaer egho konong at taka ok sva vraekae', the Svear have the right to take a king and to cast him out: the older Vastgota law, about 1220 (Collin and Schlyter 1827; gloss ours): LATER. Mark, ore and ortug (8 and 24) and the low price of a foreigner's life are from the same law and peoples/svea_gotlandic.md. That the king must ask the people: Rimbert c. 26 (Robinson 1921), of 852.

people.name: Sibbi
people.trait: A fowler who came down from the fells as a boy: he nets crane and duck on the plain, watches the boats for a share, and knows where the river will be next week.
people.want: A hawk of his own, and for the plain to stay wet, which it will not.
people.fear: The dry years. Each spring the flood is a little less and the cranes stand a little further off.
people.voice: Quiet, sideways. Answers a question about one thing with a fact about birds, and the fact is the answer.
people.looks: Late twenties, lean and wind-brown, hair tied back with a thong, a hooded short cloak of grey wadmal, skin leggings wet to the thigh, a coiled net on one shoulder and a brace of duck on the other.
knows: how high a boat can go on this water this month, to a hand's breadth
the way over the plain in flood, and over the ice, and when the ice will not bear
the white birds of the fells, and a riddle about what falls on them
who came up the river before you and what they carried

ties.note: A place by her fire for the first cranes of the year.
A cow taken from his father by the lawman's judgement. A small feud, kept warm.
His mother's kinsman on the old island takes ships through the sounds below Birka. Between them they know the water from the sea to the mounds.
In winter he traps for a man who sells east. The best skins never see the sledge market.
He brings down for her that she has not asked for.

lines.greet: Your boat draws a hand too much for the upper reach. Leave her here. The cranes left here too, this morning.
lines.greet_again: The water is down two fingers since you came last. Same place. I kept the willow clear for you.
lines.greet_friend: I saw your sail from the middle mound. I am not supposed to stand on it. Nobody saw.
rumour: When the teal go south before the birch turns, the bay shuts early. They went six days ago.
In the fells the hens are brown in summer and white in winter. So is what falls on them. I can make a riddle of that. I did.
Two sledges of marten came down last night and did not stop at the market. Somebody at Birka has paid already.
lines.saying: The bird that calls is not the one in the net.
lines.farewell: Keep the three hills behind your left shoulder until the river bends. After that, ask the water.

people.source: invented; 'a fowler from the fells' who gives r-gest-20 (riddles_793.json: he snares ptarmigan in winter). The land was rising and the place slowly lost its water (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala). Hawking with a lord here: town_games_793.json.

people.name: Ingirun
people.trait: The best weaver in the sunk houses: makes the household's cloth as dues and sells what is over, and can tell Frisian cloth from English with her eyes shut.
people.want: Good dye and a buyer who is not the estate: madder, woad, and a Frisian who comes back.
people.fear: Her eyes going, as her mother's did at the loom in a house with no light.
people.voice: Measures as she talks: so many threads, so many ells. Says each count once to you and once to herself.
people.looks: Early twenties, slight, red-knuckled, fair hair under a linen cloth, a blue strap dress of her own weaving on two small bronze brooches, a bone weaving-sword in her hand, lint on everything.
knows: what cloth the household wants and what it will give: iron, wax or squirrel, never silver
the price of madder and woad here, which is whatever she can pay
which house in the row smiths, and who is setting red stones in gold for the high seat (?)
what her aunt at the hearth will not say about the old roof

ties.note: Her mother's sister, who chose the loom for her.
She has noticed the down. She has not said so.
Cloth down the river for beads up it, by any boat that will carry a bundle unopened.
He stood her a sack of madder against next winter's cloth. He has it written on a stick.

lines.greet: Frisian cloth? Let me feel it. Do not tell me where it is from. I will tell you.
lines.greet_again: Forty threads to the thumb, your last bolt. I counted. Forty. Bring that again and I will find iron for it.
lines.greet_friend: I wove a border with your boat in it. Small. You would have to know it was there.
rumour: The household pays me in what it has. Bring madder and I will pay you in what I have: wadmal that keeps out the sea.
A man in the third house sets red stones in gold, so fine you cannot see the cells. He works for one buyer only.
They took the good hangings out of the hall last week. All of them. Nobody takes hangings down for a feast.
lines.saying: Count the threads before the cloth is cut. After, count your losses.
lines.farewell: Bring dye. Red, if the Franks will sell it. Go well.

people.source: invented; weaving in the pit houses (sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala_fornlämningsområde). The garnet workshop on the terrace is unchecked (dossier, section 8) (?). madder, woad, wadmal and frisian_cloth are goods_793.json.

people.name: Arnfast
people.trait: The king's skald two lifetimes after Vifast and of his kin: quicker, poorer, and the keeper of a chain of five sticks whose end he has never dared follow.
people.want: Somebody else to carry the chain round the sea and tell him whether the old man's last stick tells the truth.
people.fear: The water. He was in a boat off Gotland once and has made verses about staying ashore ever since.
people.voice: Starts in the middle and counts backwards to the start. Laughs first, then counts whether it was worth laughing.
people.looks: About thirty-five, small and quick, a short dark beard, an eastern coat with a silk band at the cuffs that has seen better silk, a rune stick behind one ear like a carpenter's wedge.
knows: the first stick of Delling's door, for eight pennyweights, and that the last one is found, not bought
which skippers have been to the Gotland beaches and the river of the east
that weights are now made to the measure of the caliphs' coin, and where to get a true set
what the old skald said about a Frisian house, if yours is the house

ties.note: His mother's father's father. He has the tally sticks and cannot read all the notches.
The wright at the Gotlanders' slip took the second stick for a charm against rot and laid it under a keel. The island's skald has it off him now, and the wright wants it back.
A Svea poet in the east holds the third and claims to have made it.
The pilot at the river mouth in Skane carried him home sick from the sea, and holds the fourth stick against the fare.
Birka's poets have sold the sea's daughters to merchants by the cup since old Grimulf's day. Arnfast says that is fishmongering.
Liknat of Gotland has the second stick now, and asks it of the benches every evening as if it were his own. He tells every harbour that Arnfast is afraid of boats.
The pilot's sister at the river mouth in Skane keeps the fourth stick in her chest, and hands it only to one who has earned the third.

lines.greet: A Frisian house. Wait. My mother's grandfather notched a Frisian. Here: one boat, four men, pays in good silver, corrects nobody. Is that you?
lines.greet_again: You again, and dry. I have never understood how you people do it. Eight pennyweights, and I will give you a door to stand before.
lines.greet_friend: Sit. I have made a verse about your boat. It rhymes with nothing, like the sea.
rumour: The father of day has a door, and things stand before it. That is all I may say for nothing.
A farmer on Gotland sleeps on more silver than the king eats off. Every Gotlander says so. Every Gotlander says it is another farmer.
Weights now go by the eastern coin. The lawman's set is true. The set at Birka is true on market days.
lines.saying: I have praised many ships. From the shore. That is where praise is safest.
lines.farewell: Go round the sea for me and come back. I will be here. I am always here.

people.source: invented; 'a skald of the Svear king' who sells r-vafth-24 from 871 and with whom r-vafth-52 is found (riddles_793.json, set dellings_door: Uppsalir, Paviken or Birka, Aldeigjuborg, Ahus and back; reward rw_hoard_spillings). Weights to the dirham's standard: Design/content/realms/sweden_gotland.md, 870s.

people.name: Sigvid
people.trait: A farmer's son of Uppsalir who has been to England and come home with silver and a by-name: the England-farer. Generous, loud, and not at ease on his own land.
people.want: A stone for his father that will be read when the mounds are forgotten, and someone to tell him what the English silver is truly worth.
people.fear: That he was away when his father died, and that the stone says so to anyone who can read.
people.voice: Norse with English words for coin and weather. Tells the same three stories and each time the river at London is wider.
people.looks: About thirty-five, big, a sea-bleached beard, an English cloak of good red wool with a round silver brooch, a small cross and a small hammer on one thong, a purse he keeps a hand on.
knows: the English ports and what tribute silver buys there and here
which moneyer's pennies are good: he has a bagful and has bitten most of them
who else in Uppland took the silver, and under which leader
the price of a rune stone and the name of the man who cuts a clean snake

ties.note: He took silver in England in the years the tall Dane led the fleet. Whether under him the stone does not say (the game's link) (?)
After 1016 the silver he remembers was Cnut's.
He left London with a debt at Eadwold the moneyer's bench, and has meant to send it for ten years.
His sons will stand with the bishop's few at Sigtuna. He himself hedged: one thong, two gods.
The jarl who holds the eastern river town for the king's daughter sends to him when he wants to know what an English penny is worth.

lines.greet: You are from the south. Good. Look at this penny and tell me the king's name on it. I know it. I want to hear you say it.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian! I told my wife about the river at London again. She says it has grown since Yule.
lines.greet_friend: Stand here while the cutter works. You can read. Tell me he has spelled my father right.
rumour: They pay you to go away, the English. Then another fleet comes and they pay that one. I have never seen a people so rich or so tired.
The king here is baptised and the feast here is kept. Both. I wear both. A man should not be poorer in gods than in silver.
The mint at the new town strikes the king's name. An Englishman cut the dies. He cannot say the name he cuts.
lines.saying: I went far for silver. The stone is so that someone knows where I came back to.
lines.farewell: Go well. If you lie at London, look for a moneyer who curses the Svear. Give him my greeting, not my name.

people.source: Rundata U 978, in the wall of Gamla Uppsala church: Sigvid the England-farer raised the stone for Vedjarf his father (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppland_Runic_Inscription_978). Real name, by-name and father; his years, faith, looks, debt and every word are invented. Uppland men who took geld in England: U 344 (Ulf of Borresta). Sigtuna's pennies with English die-cutters: chronicle_793.json 995-sigtuna-coins.

people.name: Adalvard
people.trait: Adalvard the Younger, sent from Bremen to be bishop at Sigtuna: learned, burning, and sure that one fire at Uppsalir would bring the whole people to the font.
people.want: The holy place at Uppsalir closed or burned, and the king's leave to do it.
people.fear: That he will be sent away with nothing done, and that Bremen will hear of it from someone else first.
people.voice: Saxon-accented Norse, careful and a little loud. Quotes, then explains the quotation.
people.looks: About forty, spare, tonsured, a clean-shaven long face, a dark travelling cloak over a white alb, a plain bishop's ring, a small book in a leather satchel at his side.
knows: who in Sigtuna is baptised, and who is baptised only in Sigtuna
what the king said when he was asked for the fire, word for word
the road to the western Gotar, where a bishop is safe
what a book costs and what a bell costs, and that he has neither

ties.note: The England-farer's sons are of his flock; the father is in his prayers.
Bishop Egino's man in Skane: the two bishops made the plan against Uppsalir together.
Two hundred years dead. Adalvard has read the Life and means to finish what it began.

lines.greet: A Christian from the Rhine mouth. God sent you, or the wind did. Have you room in your boat for a chest of books, going either way?
lines.greet_again: You come and go freely. I am told where I may stand. Tell me what they say of me at Uppsalir.
lines.greet_friend: I will say Mass at first light for those who sail. For you I will say it whether you come or not.
rumour: I asked the king for leave to burn it. He said they would kill me and cast him out. He said it kindly.
In a ninth year a Christian here pays silver to stay away from the feast. They call it a fine. I call it the cheapest thing they sell.
A man of my church told me what hangs in that grove. I will not tell you. I wrote it to Bremen.
lines.saying: The apostle did not ask leave of the Ephesians.
lines.farewell: God keep you on the water. If I am gone when you return, ask for me among the western Gotar.

people.source: Adalvard the Younger, bishop at Sigtuna in the 1060s: he and Egino of Skane planned to destroy the temple, King Stenkil refused, and he withdrew to Vastergotland; in Bremen June 1069, dead by 1072 (Adam of Bremen IV.30, by way of en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adalvard_the_Younger; dossier, section 3). His birth year, looks and words are invented (?). The buying-off is Adam IV.27. Nothing of Adam is quoted.

stories.title: The count of the lay
stories.summary: The Svear king's skald sells the questions of the giant's lay one stanza at a time, and has a standing quarrel with the Danes' poet at Hleidr over whose version is true. He wants a stick carried between the halls by someone who will not read it; Ravn, if he is aboard, sat a winter on this bench and knows what is on it without looking.
stories.picture: A dim hall by firelight: a tall stooped man with a plaited beard holding out a notched stick across the fire to a Frisian merchant, a grey-haired seaman behind the merchant looking at the floor.

beats.text: Vifast sells the giant's questions at six pennyweights and the High One's at eight. A guest who answers one before the bench drinks free; one who cannot, drinks and pays.
Sit up with Gillaug when she banks the fire and she gives the riddle of the embers for nothing (r-gest-33), and says who has been selling it.
Sibbi the fowler gives the riddle of what falls white on the fells (r-gest-20) to anyone who lets him ride down to Birka and back.

beats.when: year >= 793 and year < 825 and not flag.uppsalir_stick_carried
beats.text: Vifast cuts a stick for the poet at Hleidr: his count of the lay, fifty-five, and one stanza the Danes have wrong. He asks that it go unread.

Thorulf reads the stick aloud to the bench, laughs, and cuts an answer on the back of it. He asks whether the merchant read the front. Ravn, if he is there, says the count is right and the stanza is not wrong, only older.
The skald at Birka offers twelve pennyweights for a look at either side of the stick before it goes on.
With the last question known from Ravn, the merchant may stand before the Svear bench and be asked it (r-vafth-54). The only true answer is that no man knows.
The stick comes home with the Danes' answer cut on its back: nine notches and a stanza. Vifast counts it again that night, when nobody is watching him do it.

The stone-cutter on Gotland sends the Svear king's skald a riddle by any boat going up the bay, and gets a verse back. Neither will say who is ahead. He asks whether you are a man who carries sticks unread.

endings.how: You carried the stick to Hleidr and the answer back, and showed neither to anyone.
endings.text: Vifast counts the notches on the answer twice and says nothing for a while. Then he moves you one place up the bench. The quarrel between the halls goes on, as both poets wish, and goes on by your boat.
endings.reward: Sets uppsalir_stick_unread; deed carried_letters; about 300 d in weighed silver over three calls; Vifast and Thorulf both friendly; the stanzas here at half weight for life.

endings.how: You let the Birka skald, or Ravn, read the stick on the way.
endings.text: By the next thing every hall on the lake has the stanza, and each has it a little different. Vifast knows who carried it. He sells to you still, at the full weight, and seats you by the door.
endings.reward: Sets uppsalir_stick_read; 12 d at once and the stanza itself (give_text t-vafth-29); the Birka skald a fast friend; Vifast wary.

endings.how: You brought the last question from Ravn and gave the true answer before the bench.
endings.text: The hall is quiet. The king, a shape beyond the fire, sends down his own horn. Vifast cuts one more notch, the first in years, and says the count is now fifty-five and one guest.
endings.reward: rw_favour_uppsalir (riddles_793.json): deed won_great_riddle and the king's lasting favour in Svealand, fewer searches by his men; about 900 d in rings; sets rd_setter_known.

stories.reward: A place on the Svear bench, the hall's stanzas cheap, two riddles given for kindness, and for the one who brings the last question, the king's lasting favour.

stories.title: Delling's door
stories.summary: From 871 the king's skald Arnfast sells the first of five sticks that hang together by a word: the father of day, a door, the sun and the wolf behind her. The others are held on a Gotland beach, on the river of the east and at a river mouth in Skane, and the last is found back here; together they say where a great weight of silver lies under a floor on Gotland.
stories.picture: Five rune sticks laid in a fan on a ship's thwart, a folding scale beside them, and beyond the gunwale a low grey island under a pale sun with a darker patch of cloud close behind it.

beats.text: Arnfast sells the first stick for eight pennyweights (r-vafth-24): who is the father of day. He says the last stick cannot be bought and that he has never seen the end himself.

A Gotland shipwright kept the second stick under a keel as a charm against rot; the island's skald has it now, and asks it each evening in the shelter above the beach (r-gest-08). It opens with the word the first one answered. Before 976 the same stick may be had at Birka.
A Svea poet on the eastern river has the third (r-gest-15): what stands before the same door and is chased across the sky.
The pilot at the river mouth in Skane holds the fourth (r-vafth-46) against a fare the skald never paid. He will give it for the fare, or for a passage north.

With four answered, the fifth is found and not bought (r-vafth-52): Arnfast walks the merchant up the middle mound at sunrise and tells what his mother's grandfather notched last. It names a farm in the north-east of Gotland.
The farm is real and so is the farmer. He is a shipowner, his floor is new, and he is at home.

endings.how: You went to the farm with a spade while the farmer was at sea.
endings.text: Sixty-seven kilograms is more than your boat should carry and more than you can spend unseen. The Gotlanders have a law of their own for thieves and no king to appeal to. You are rich, and you do not land on that island again.
endings.reward: rw_hoard_spillings by open_fetch: a huge weight of silver, some of it bad; sets uppsalir_door_lifted; Gotland ports shunned for a generation; Arnfast will not speak of it.

endings.how: You told the farmer what five sticks say about his floor.
endings.text: He listens without moving. Then he pays you to forget it, well, and asks who else has the sticks. Within the year the second and fourth are in his chest and the chain is broken. The silver stays where it is, for eleven hundred years.
endings.reward: About 1,200 d in arm-rings; sets uppsalir_door_told; the farmer a fast friend and a host on Gotland; toll-free landing at Paviken through him.

endings.how: You brought the five answers back to Arnfast and left the floor alone.
endings.text: He makes a verse of it in which he sails round the sea himself. The king hears it and laughs, and asks who truly went. Arnfast, to his credit, points.
endings.reward: Deed won_great_riddle; sets uppsalir_door_kept; about 500 d from the king's hand; Arnfast a fast friend; the standing of a guest of the Svear hall for the house and its heir.

stories.reward: Five riddles solved in four ports, and at the end a choice between a hoard, a friend on Gotland or a name at the Svear king's table.

stories.title: The house fired to brick
stories.summary: The old hall is two hundred years old and somebody has decided it will not be mended. Before it burns the hearth-keeper wants its fire carried, alive, to the hearth of the house that will stand after it, and the smiths want iron for the new posts. Nobody tells a stranger why a king's hall is burned; a stranger who helps is told a little.
stories.picture: Night: a huge hall burning end to end on a high bank, the whole plain lit red, and in the foreground a broad woman walking away from it carrying a lidded pot in both hands, a merchant beside her shielding it from the wind.

beats.text: Ingirun says the hangings have been taken down from the hall, all of them. In the next house a smith is curling iron bars into spirals and wants more bar iron than the estate has.
Gillaug asks for a soapstone pot with a lid, the kind the Northmen of the west sell, big enough to keep embers alive for a night and a day.
Soapstone pots are had at the Vestfold market, or from any Northman skipper at Birka or Sliesthorp for twice the price.

On a still night after the harvest the household walks out of the hall with what it means to keep. The doors are wedged open. The king puts the torch to it himself, or a man does it for him: from where a stranger stands, it cannot be seen which.
The fire from the old hearth burns on the new one. Gillaug shows the place by it where the pot stood, and says whose pot it was.

A Northman skipper in the strangers' booths at Birka has soapstone pots from the west under his thwarts, lidded ones among them, at twice what they cost in Vestfold. He does not ask what a Frisian wants with a pot that keeps embers.
On the old island the caster says the hall at the mounds still owes him for its cauldron chain. He made it to last longer than the roof, he says, and from what skippers tell him of the roof, it will.

endings.how: You brought the pot and walked beside her with it on the night.
endings.text: The embers go from the old hearth to the new without going out. Nobody thanks you where others can hear. After that there is a place by the fire that is yours, and your heir is shown it.
endings.reward: Sets uppsalir_embers_carried; Gillaug a fast friend and her heir after her; lodging and provisions free here for the house; about 200 d in iron and wadmal; r-gest-33 given.

endings.how: You brought bar iron for the spirals and stayed away on the night.
endings.text: The new house's posts stand on iron curled like fern heads, as the old ones did, and some of it came in your boat. The smiths remember, and so does the steward of the dues.
endings.reward: Sets uppsalir_iron_brought; about 350 d: bar iron is paid here at half again its weight in squirrel and marten; act:fit_upgrade in the sunk houses at cost.

endings.how: You were elsewhere, and came back to a burnt terrace.
endings.text: The floor is red and hard and the nettles are already up. Gillaug kept the fire in an iron kettle and burned her hands. She does not blame you, and tells you so, twice.
endings.reward: Nothing lost: the tale of the burning from three mouths that do not agree, and one of them is news worth a meal in any hall on the lake.

stories.reward: A place by the Svear king's fire that passes to your heir, or the smiths' goodwill and a good price for iron.

stories.title: The ninth year
stories.summary: About the spring equinox of a ninth year all the Svear come to Uppsalir for a feast nine days long, and nobody is excused: a Christian pays silver to stay away. The merchant is baptised, his crew is mixed, and the lawman wants to know before the first day where the Frisian will be standing.
stories.picture: A crowd of fur-capped men seen from behind, all facing a dark stand of old trees in snow; in the foreground a lawman holding out an open scale pan to a merchant, who has a hand on his purse.

beats.text: Holmgeir says it plainly: in the ninth year everyone comes or pays. He names the weight for a stranger who holds another god. It is not small and it is not ruinous.
The crew splits. Ravn says a man should see a thing before he judges it. Beornwine will not go near the trees and asks to wait at the boat.
The path to the old trees is roped. What is done there in those nine days the game does not show: a stranger who pays hears songs he is glad not to follow, far off, and sees the crows.
The few baptised at Birka ask what the Frisian did at Uppsalir. Herigar asks without looking up from his tallies; the widow Frideburg asks looking straight at you.
A priest at home has heard, from someone, where the merchant was at the equinox. Penance, or thanks, by what was done.

Two hundred years on, a bishop from Bremen sits in the king's new town and calls the fine for staying away the cheapest thing the Svear sell. He means to end the feast. The king has told him what would end first.

endings.how: You weighed out the fine to the lawman and kept to the guest house for nine days.
endings.text: The silver goes into the pan and Holmgeir tries it twice. Nobody thinks worse of you: it is the law, and you kept it. At Birka the Christians nod. Nine days is a long time to hear a feast through a wall.
endings.reward: Sets uppsalir_bought_off; costs about 60 d and nine days; deed fair_dealing among the Svear; cast.herigar and cast.frideburg friendly; no penance at home.

endings.how: You went with the people and stood where a guest stands.
endings.text: You are a guest of the whole people for nine days and eat at the king's cost. What you saw you do not tell the crew. Beornwine does not ask. The priest at home does.
endings.reward: Sets uppsalir_stood_feast; standing in Svealand rises a step and the lawman is a fast friend; morale falls among Christian hands; a penance at home (alms of about 120 d, or a fast and a cool bishop).

endings.how: You heard the year named and kept your boat at Birka until the moon after.
endings.text: No fine and no feast. You lose the best market of nine years, when every Svea with a skin to sell is at Uppsalir. Holmgeir notes who was absent, as he notes everything, without heat.
endings.reward: Nothing gained or lost but the trade; sets uppsalir_feast_missed; the lawman says so once at your next coming and then lets it lie.

stories.reward: A clean name with the lawman and Birka's Christians, or a guest's standing with the whole people at a price paid at home.

stories.title: The England-farer's stone
stories.summary: After 1012 Sigvid is home from England with a bag of tribute pennies, a debt he left at a London moneyer's bench and a father who died while he was away. He wants a stone cut, his silver judged by someone who knows English coin, and, though he would not say so, the debt off his mind before the stone goes up.
stories.picture: A tall red-grey boulder lying on trestles in a grave field, a carver chipping a snake of runes along it, a big man in a red English cloak watching, a merchant beside him holding a penny up to the light.

beats.text: Sigvid tips English pennies onto a cloak and asks which are good. Some carry the king's head and are true; some are light, and he does not want to hear which.
The moneyer at the new town will take the English silver for the king's own pennies at a loss he names. A merchant who knows both coins can do better for Sigvid, or for himself.
A moneyer at London remembers a big Svea who left owing forty pennies and a promise. He has told the story so often that the forty have become sixty.
The carver wants the words. Sigvid cannot read and asks the merchant to stand by and say whether his father's name is cut right: Vedjarf.

The jarl who holds the eastern river town asks every western skipper what an English penny is worth this year. When the answers differ he sends to a man at Uppsalir who went to England and came home with its silver. You could carry the question.

endings.how: You carried the forty pennies to the moneyer in London and brought back his word.
endings.text: The moneyer bites every one, finds them his own striking, and laughs until he coughs. The stone goes up with a clear mind behind it. Sigvid names your house at the stone-ale, and his sons remember the name.
endings.reward: Sets uppsalir_debt_carried; deeds carried_letters and kept_commission; about 400 d; Sigvid and his sons fast friends: a host at Uppsalir and Sigtuna to 1066; the London moneyer friendly.

endings.how: You sorted his pennies truly, good from light, and took a fair share for it.
endings.text: A third of the bag is light. He is silent, then says the English cheated him, then says he had rather know. He pays the carver in the good ones and keeps the light ones to pay the king.
endings.reward: Sets en_followed_silver; deed fair_dealing; about 250 d; you learn which English moneyers' names to trust (the loss at act:change_coin on English coin is less).

endings.how: You told him the good pennies were light and bought them cheap.
endings.text: You make a hundred and eighty pennies in an afternoon. At Sigtuna the moneyer weighs what Sigvid has left and tells him what he had. The stone still goes up. Your name is not spoken at the ale, and that is noticed.
endings.reward: About 180 d at once; Sigvid and his kin shunned to you; standing in Svealand falls a step; no host at Sigtuna.

stories.reward: A host among the Svear for the rest of the game's years, and a true knowledge of English coin, or a quick profit and a closed door.

works.name: A shed at the boat place
works.what: A long turf-roofed shed on posts at the landing, open to the water, where a boat can be drawn in on rollers and goods lie dry and watched until they are carried up.
works.picture: A low turf-roofed shed on a clay river bank with a small clinker boat half inside it, willows, and three mounds far off on the skyline.
works.needs: A host among the Svear, and the fowler or his heir friendly, since he will keep it.
works.gives: The boat may be laid up here over winter at no cost and is not robbed; goods may be stored at the landing; loading takes half the time. An instance of works_793.json boat_shed.
works.source: works_793.json boat_shed (240 d, 30 days). Boat houses are known all over the north; none has been found here, where even the landing place is not known (?)

works.name: A sledge, a horse and a set of bone skates
works.what: A good sledge with iron-shod runners and a small shaggy horse used to ice, kept for you at the bay's edge by a farmer, with skates of horse bone for the men.
works.picture: A shaggy horse harnessed to a loaded sledge on white lake ice, two men on bone skates poling themselves along beside it, their breath smoking.
works.needs: A boat laid up for the winter at Birka, Helgo or the landing here, and a host to answer for you.
works.gives: Uppsalir can be reached while the bay is frozen: the late-winter thing and the sledge market open to you, when iron and furs are cheapest. The horse must be fed each winter (about 12 d).
works.source: The late-winter thing and market were reached over the ice (Snorri: LATER; Design/content/realms/sweden_gotland.md). Bone skates and iron-shod sledge runners are common finds at Birka (?)

works.name: A plank way over the wet plain
works.what: Bundles of brushwood pegged down across the soft ground from the boat place to the ridge, with split logs laid over them along the line of the old posts.
works.picture: Men laying split logs across flooded grass beside a row of tall grey posts, a loaded cart waiting, three mounds ahead.
works.needs: The lawman's leave, given at the thing, and a dry month after the hay.
works.gives: Carts reach the estate in any season but deep flood: carrying up takes half the time, and the household's steward counts it as a gift to the king. An instance of works_793.json causeway.
works.source: works_793.json causeway (300 d, 45 days). Brushwood and plank ways over wet ground are the north's ordinary road-making; none has been found on this plain (?)

works.name: A bridge for a soul
works.what: A causeway of stone and gravel over the wet place on the road to the landing, with a rune stone beside it that names your dead and says the bridge was made for their souls.
works.picture: A low stone causeway over a marshy stream with a tall rune stone at its end, a cross cut in the middle of the snake of runes, a woman leading a horse across.
works.needs: A dead kinsman or partner to name, and a carver; a Christian house, or one willing to be taken for one.
works.gives: As unlocks_793.json unlock_work_uppsalir_bridge: carters reach the landing in wet weather and the market is better stocked in spring and autumn; your dead are named on the stone; 20 d a year to keep.
works.source: The Jarlabanki stones at Taby, about 1050 (U 127, U 164, U 212, U 261); women building bridges for souls (So 101, U 489); unlocks_793.json; works_793.json bridge_share

works.name: A stone by the road
works.what: A boulder of red-grey granite set upright by the path through the grave field, a band of runes cut along it in the shape of a snake and blacked: who raised it, for whom, and where he had been.
works.picture: A carver on his knees chipping runes into a tall boulder by a path among grave mounds, a pot of black beside him.
works.needs: A carver (Sigvid knows one), and someone of the house dead or far away.
works.gives: The house's name stands at Uppsalir: an heir is known here on his first coming. An instance of works_793.json rune_stone.
works.source: works_793.json rune_stone (300 d, 40 days); most Uppland stones are of 1000-1100 (peoples/svea_gotlandic.md); U 978 stands here

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The lake boat of the Svear: nine or ten paces, four or five pairs of oars, light enough for six men to drag past a shoal. The wrights under the boat hill build them of split oak, and build the same boat for the dead.
ships.picture: A slim clinker boat in frame under an open shed by a small river, a steep grass hill with boat-shaped hollows behind it.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json norse_small_boat; the Viks boat, 9.6 by 2.2 m, about 1050 (sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viksbåten); the boat graves of Valsgarde. That they were built here is inference (?): story/ships_793.json does not list uppsalir under built_at.

ships.note: There is always a six-oared boat for sale at the boat place after the thing, when a man has sold his goods and would rather ride home. The fowler knows whose and what is wrong with her.
ships.picture: A weathered six-oared boat drawn up among willows on a clay bank, a sledge lying on its side beside her.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json norse_small_boat; traffic_793.json uppsalir (river and local boats)

ships.note: A hollowed trunk for the upper river, the fowler's kind: she carries two men and a net, or one man and four sacks, over water a hand deep.
ships.picture: A man poling a dug-out through flooded grass, cranes rising ahead of him.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json logboat; the shallow river and the wet plain (dossier, section 1)

ships.note: Nothing of this size is built or lies here: no ship of size comes above the bay. A man with the king's favour may be given the use of a ship of the summer's muster, lying at Birka or, after 980, at Sigtuna, with her crew, for a share.
ships.picture: A fifteen-pace ship with a striped sail lying at a jetty of a lake town, shields along her rail, a steward on the quay pointing a merchant aboard.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json norse_allround_ship; traffic_793.json uppsalir. Ships, crews and steersmen for the summer were settled at this thing by the Uppland law of 1296: LATER (dossier, section 4). The loan is the game's (?)

sayings.text: The control of public business of every kind should rest with the whole people and not with the king.
sayings.source: King Olaf's answer to Anskar, about 852: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 26 (tr. C. H. Robinson 1921), as given in Design/content/spine.md. Said at Birka; held true here.

sayings.text: Wits must he have who wanders wide, but all is easy at home; at the witless man the wise shall wink when among such men he sits.
sayings.source: Havamal 5 (Bellows 1923; texts_793.json havamal_005; written down about 1270, older in substance)

sayings.text: Away from his arms in the open field a man should fare not a foot; for never he knows when the need for a spear shall arise on the distant road.
Cattle die, and kinsmen die, and so one dies one's self; one thing now that never dies, the fame of a dead man's deeds.
sayings.source: Havamal 77 (Bellows 1923; texts_793.json havamal_077). Said on the mounds.

sayings.text: Give praise to the day at evening, to ice when it is crossed, to ale that is drunk.
sayings.source: Havamal 81, in part (Bellows 1923; texts_793.json havamal_081). Said by anyone who has come to the thing by sledge.

sayings.text: So may the gods be kind to me.
sayings.source: 'Sva se maer guth hull', the oath of the older Vastgota law, about 1220, which kept a heathen plural in a Christian book (Collin and Schlyter 1827; gloss ours): LATER

sayings.text: Count it at the buying, count it at the selling, and weigh it in between.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: a Svea counts everything twice (spine, tone)

sayings.text: A Frisian asked how far it was from the boats to the king. 'In my grandfather's day, a spear's throw,' said the fowler. 'Now, a wet walk. Your grandson should bring a horse.'
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the land was rising and the place slowly lost its water (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala)

sayings.text: A Dane came up the river for the king's seat and got the king's field. It is a big field. He has all of it he needs.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, for the years after about 985: a Northman's understatement on the battle on the plain (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fyrisvellir)

sayings.text: They asked the skald how many kings lie in the mounds. 'Three,' he said. 'And in the lays?' 'More. The lays have more room.'
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; whose bones are in the mounds is not known (dossier, section 8)

sayings.text: If our gods are too few for you, we can make you another out of a dead king.
sayings.source: A turn on the gods' message to the Svear, about 852, that they would take the dead King Eric among them: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 26 (Robinson 1921). The turn is invented; from 852.

easter_eggs.text: On the top of the eastern mound a child's game is scratched in the turf: a square of squares with a king in the middle. Under the turf, in a clay pot of burnt bone, lie the pieces of a real one.
easter_eggs.source: A tafl set went on the pyre in the east mound, opened by B. E. Hildebrand in 1846 by a tunnel 25 m long; ivory gaming pieces in the west mound, opened 1874 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala)

easter_eggs.text: Count the posts across the plain and the stumps between them, and pace the gaps: a hundred and forty-four, five or six paces apart. Twelve twelves. The lawman, who counts everything twice, has never counted these.
easter_eggs.source: The post row found 2012-2013: 144 posts over about a kilometre (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_at_Uppsala). Whether any stood in 793 is unknown (?)

easter_eggs.text: After a hard rain something yellow shows in the mud of the plain and a Svea gets down from his horse to look. It is a buttercup. The skald says that is how a Dane once got away from a king.
easter_eggs.source: Hrolf Kraki strewing gold on the plain so that the Svear dismounted to gather it; poets call gold 'the seed of the Fyris fields' (Snorri, Skaldskaparmal, about 1220, by way of en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyrisvellir): LATER

easter_eggs.text: A man in the sunk houses is asked whose hall it is. He says: the god's, who built it and gave it all his land and dues. Which god? He looks at you as if you had asked whose sky it is.
easter_eggs.source: Snorri says Frey built the temple and gave it his lands, the beginning of the kings' estate (Ynglinga saga, Laing 1844, by way of en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppsala_öd): LATER

easter_eggs.text: Kick the red floor of the burnt terrace and it rings like a pot. Break off a piece and it is brick, a thing no Svea knows how to make on purpose.
easter_eggs.source: The hall burned so hot that the clay of its walls was fired to brick (sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala_fornlämningsområde)

easter_eggs.text: From about 985 a Danish skipper, asked about the fight on the plain, says only that a man he knew did not flee at Uppsala. He says it as the best thing that can be said of anyone.
easter_eggs.source: The Hallestad stone, DR 295, in Skane: raised for Toki Gormsson, who 'did not flee at Uppsala' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fyrisvellir; runes_793.json)

easter_eggs.text: In the years after 985 an Icelander in the king's house is paid in silver for two verses about the ravens on the plain. He is the only man in this file whose own words about Uppsalir survive, and they are about what the birds ate.
easter_eggs.source: Thorvald Hjaltason's two stanzas on the battle, kept in a late tale (Styrbjarnar thattr), by way of en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fyrisvellir: LATER; not quoted

easter_eggs.text: Ask anyone here about the house roofed with gold and the chain on its gable and they ask where you heard it. From a Saxon? A Saxon who had been here? No. They thought not.
easter_eggs.source: Adam of Bremen IV.26 and the notes added to it, about 1075, second hand: no such building has been found (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_at_Uppsala; dossier, section 8). Never shown.

easter_eggs.text: Sigvid's stone has a snake of runes and his father's name. In nine hundred years it will be built into the wall of a stone church on this spot, facing outward, as if the church were reading it.
easter_eggs.source: U 978, in the outer wall of Gamla Uppsala church (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppland_Runic_Inscription_978); the stone church is of the mid 1100s

easter_eggs.text: The wrights under the boat hill will not say how many boats are in the hill. More than they have launched this year. The oldest went in when the great mounds were new, and the last has not gone in yet.
easter_eggs.source: Valsgarde: boat graves from the 500s to the 1000s, one great family's burial ground (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valsgärde)

easter_eggs.text: After 1050 a stone at the new town is raised by 'the Frisians' guild-brothers' for a brother named Thorkel. Not one name on it is Frisian. Your house may be the only Frisians who ever sat at that drinking.
easter_eggs.source: Rundata U 379, Sigtuna (runes_793.json sigtuna_u379); unlocks_793.json unlock_title_frisian_guild

unlocks.how: Lodge at the guest house on two calls and give a gift at table once (act:gift), or end uppsalir.embers by carrying the fire.
unlocks.gives: The lawman weighs for you and the thing's peace covers you as far as the boats: act:lawsuit and act:witness open at the flat mound, and a stranger's low price no longer applies to you in a quarrel.

unlocks.what: The fowler's marks for the river
unlocks.how: Be friendly with Sibbi, or give him passage to Birka and back once.
unlocks.gives: The boat is told to the hand's breadth how high she can go this month; no grounding on the river; counts as one of the three passages for unlocks_793.json unlock_pilot_malaren.
Uppsalir can be visited while the bay is frozen (ice and month of the late-winter thing): the sledge market's prices for bar_iron, squirrel, marten and beaver are the year's lowest.

unlocks.how: Have Holmgeir or his heir try your scales (act:test_silver at the sledge market, with a small gift).
unlocks.gives: Sets sv_scale if the house has not got it: northern buyers stop cheating on the weight. From 871 the set agrees with the eastern coin as well.

unlocks.what: A place on the skald's left
unlocks.how: Buy three stanzas, or answer one riddle before the bench, or end uppsalir.older_lays by the ending 'unread'.
unlocks.gives: The hall's stanzas at half weight; act:riddles and act:song at the hall cost nothing; the skald says what the king thinks of you before an audience.

unlocks.how: Answer the last question before the bench (uppsalir.older_lays, ending 'the_question'), or end uppsalir.dellings_door by keeping the chain.
unlocks.gives: riddles_793.json rw_favour_uppsalir: deed won_great_riddle and a lasting rise in Svealand; fewer searches by the king's men at Birka; the hire of a ship of the muster (ships: norse_allround_ship).

unlocks.how: End uppsalir.embers by carrying the fire.
unlocks.gives: act:lodge and act:provision at the guest house cost nothing for the house and its heirs; act:rumours there gives the household's news a week before the market has it.

unlocks.how: End uppsalir.embers by bringing the iron, or sell bar_iron in the sunk houses on three calls.
unlocks.gives: act:buy_at_source in the sunk houses for iron_tools, rivets and spearheads at the maker's price; act:fit_upgrade there at cost.

unlocks.what: Known to keep the law of the ninth year
unlocks.how: End uppsalir.ninth_year by paying the fine.
unlocks.gives: Deed fair_dealing among the Svear; the baptised at Birka (cast.herigar, cast.frideburg) take the house for one of theirs; no card asks again where you stood.

unlocks.how: End uppsalir.england_silver by carrying the debt or judging the silver truly.
unlocks.gives: A host at Uppsalir and Sigtuna from 1012 to 1066; the loss at act:change_coin on English silver is less; opens unlocks_793.json unlock_title_frisian_guild from 1050 without the three summers.

sources: Design/content/dossiers/uppsalir.md (6 Oct 2026): the research this file is built on. Its warnings are kept: no golden temple drawn, no number of victims given as fact, no king's name for 793, no year fixed for the hall's burning except as the game's switch, Bjorn, Olaf, Anund and Anskar not placed here, and the words Disting, Fyris and Uppsala od not put in any mouth.

Wikipedia, read for the dossier: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala ; https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala ; https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_Uppsala_fornlämningsområde ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_at_Uppsala ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fyrisvellir ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyrisvellir ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disting ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppsala_öd ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adalvard_the_Younger ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valsgärde ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppland_Runic_Inscription_978

Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, tr. C. H. Robinson, Anskar, the Apostle of the North (London 1921), c. 9-11, 19, 26-27: https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/anskar.asp . The only quoted words in this file not from the Havamal.

Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum, about 1075, I.62, II.58, IV.21, IV.26-27, IV.30: read through the pages above and the repo's lore files; chapter numbers partly unchecked (?); nothing quoted (no safe translation).

Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla (tr. S. Laing 1844), Ynglinga saga and Olaf the Saint's saga c. 77 (?); Skaldskaparmal: LATER, by way of the pages above. The Uppland law, 1296, and the older Vastgota law, about 1220 (Collin and Schlyter 1827): LATER.

The Poetic Edda, tr. H. A. Bellows (New York 1923): Havamal 5, 38, 77, 81 (texts_793.json) and the lay of Vafthruthnir (riddles_793.json r-vafth-..., texts_793.json t-vafth-...). Gestumblindi's riddles: Vigfusson and Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale (1883) (riddles_793.json r-gest-...).

Rune stones by Rundata number: U 978 (Sigvid, Gamla Uppsala), DR 295 (Hallestad), U 379 (Sigtuna, runes_793.json sigtuna_u379), U 344, U 127, U 164, U 212, U 261, So 101, U 489, So 179: read through Wikipedia's runestone pages and Design/content/peoples/svea_gotlandic.md.

The project's own files: Design/content/spine.md and spine.json (threads riddle_road, cross_and_grove, price_of_england, silver_road; the cast); Design/content/realms/sweden_gotland.md; Design/content/peoples/svea_gotlandic.md; Design/content/lore/gods_cult.md; ports_793.json, goods_793.json, riddles_793.json, texts_793.json, runes_793.json, chronicle_793.json, trade_year_793.json, traffic_793.json, story/unlocks_793.json, story/works_793.json, story/town_games_793.json.

Invented and said so: every person but Sigvid and Adalvard, and every word either of those two speaks; the guest house, the boat shed and the sheds under the boat hill; the king's lesser house after the fire; Ravn's winter on this bench; the carrying of the embers; the kinship of Gillaug to Frideburg and of Holmgeir to Holmfast; the years given to U 978 and to the hall's burning.
